messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Parata is a 53-year-old Māori-American photographer, married and based in Portland, Oregon, where he has spent the better part of two decades building a respected career in documentary and editorial work. He came to the intake session quietly, choosing the chair nearest the door without being directed to it, and sat with his back to the wall — a posture his wife has come to recognise as the version of Rangi that returned from Papua New Guinea fourteen months ago.

The event that brought him to this office occurred during an assignment in a remote highland province, where Rangi had travelled alone to document a land-rights dispute for an international magazine. On his third day in the region, he was detained by a faction of armed men connected to one of the parties in the conflict. He was held for eleven days in a concrete outbuilding with no natural light, his hands bound for long stretches, his camera equipment confiscated. His captors were unpredictable in their movements — entering without warning, sometimes in groups, sometimes alone — and the sound of footsteps approaching the door became, over those eleven days, the signal around which every moment of terror was organised. He was eventually released without physical injury following intervention by a local journalist, but the experience left a mark that no clean bill of health could address.

In the months after his return to Portland, Rangi noticed that the world had reorganised itself around threat in ways he could not fully articulate to his wife, Diane. He began scanning every person who entered a room, reading their body language for signs of intent before he had consciously decided to do so. A stranger shifting weight from foot to foot, a colleague reaching across a desk too quickly — any sudden movement by another person placed him immediately on guard, his chest tightening, his jaw clenching before his mind had caught up. He had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought and more like a fact, that dangerous people were a permanent feature of any environment, and that his survival depended on identifying them first.

This belief shaped his behaviour in ways that accumulated steadily. Before entering any space — a coffee shop, a gallery opening, a client's studio — Rangi now maps the room for exits, identifying which door he could reach fastest and what might obstruct him. He chooses his seat with care, always angling for a position that offers a sightline to the entrance and a wall at his back. His body, he reports, never fully settles. There is a baseline tension that runs through him from the moment he wakes, a readiness that does not distinguish between a crowded restaurant and an empty street.

His work has been the most visible casualty of this reorganisation. Documentary photography requires presence in unpredictable environments — markets, protests, community gatherings — and Rangi has turned down three significant commissions in the past year because he could not trust himself to function in those settings. He accepted a smaller corporate contract instead, shooting controlled interiors with known personnel, but even there he found himself asking colleagues repeatedly whether they thought the building's security was adequate, whether the neighbourhood was considered safe, whether a particular person on staff seemed "off" to them. Diane has heard variations of these questions at home for over a year. She answers them with patience, but both of them know that her reassurance holds for only a short time before the uncertainty returns.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a moment at his nephew's birthday party last month, when a child ran toward him suddenly from behind a doorway. He was across the room before he understood what had happened, heart hammering, certain for one terrible second that he was back in that outbuilding. He stood outside on the porch for twenty minutes, unable to go back in. His nephew was nine years old. Rangi told the intake clinician that he does not recognise himself in moments like that. What he is most afraid of is that this is now simply who he is. What he is most hoping for, he said after a long pause, is to be able to walk into a room and just be in it.
